output.query: Management of drug-induced QT prolongation and torsades de pointes

results.finding: In torsades de pointes, QT-prolonging drugs are stopped and intravenous magnesium sulfate (2 g) is given whether or not serum magnesium is low; potassium is kept in the high-normal range (4.5-5.0 mmol/L).
results.source: Drew BJ et al., Prevention of torsade de pointes in hospital settings: AHA/ACCF scientific statement. Circulation 2010;121:1047-1060

results.finding: Recurrent pause-dependent torsades unresponsive to magnesium can be suppressed by temporary transvenous pacing or isoproterenol infusion; ECG monitoring continues until the QTc falls below 500 ms.
results.source: Drew BJ et al., Prevention of torsade de pointes in hospital settings: AHA/ACCF scientific statement. Circulation 2010;121:1047-1060

results.finding: In drug-induced long QT, the offending drugs are withdrawn and electrolyte abnormalities corrected; QT-prolonging drugs are avoided thereafter.
results.source: Zeppenfeld K et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and the prevention of sudden cardiac death. Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997-4126

output.summary: Torsades de pointes is managed by stopping QT-prolonging drugs, intravenous magnesium, potassium repletion to the high-normal range, and pacing or isoproterenol for pause-dependent recurrence.

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: Acquired (drug-induced) long QT syndrome is the most common cause of QTc prolongation encountered in clinical practice; polypharmacy with multiple QT-prolonging agents carries additive risk that is often underappreciated when each drug is evaluated in isolation
A high-dose SSRI (citalopram), a macrolide (azithromycin) and a 5-HT3 antagonist (ondansetron) are each QT-prolonging, and their combination is particularly hazardous

Women have a longer baseline QTc than men due to sex-based differences in IKr (cardiac repolarizing potassium current) and are approximately twofold more susceptible to drug-induced torsades de pointes at equivalent drug concentrations

Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia are critical potentiating factors for drug-induced long QT; thiazide diuretics are a common cause of both electrolyte deficiencies, and illness-related poor oral intake can compound the deficit

Torsades de pointes is characteristically pause-dependent (short-long-short RR triggering) and self-terminating in most cases, but can degenerate to ventricular fibrillation; IV magnesium sulfate is the first-line treatment regardless of serum magnesium level

Convulsive syncope (brief, irregular limb movements from cerebral hypoperfusion during any syncopal episode) is frequently misinterpreted as epileptic seizure; the distinction is critical to avoid inappropriate antiepileptic drug therapy
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Five required actions (ECG, medication review, electrolytes, telemetry, TTE); two red herrings (seizure-like presentation, routine-looking polypharmacy); the agent must link the QTc, the electrolytes and the drug list to a reversible cause.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Patricia Holloway is a 60-year-old woman with a history of major depressive disorder on citalopram, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and recent community-acquired pneumonia who presents to the emergency department after a sudden loss of consciousness at home approximately 45 minutes ago. Her husband witnessed the entire event. He reports that she was standing in the kitchen, appeared to briefly sway, then suddenly became unresponsive and fell to the floor, striking the back of her head. He states she immediately exhibited rapid, irregular shaking movements of her limbs, lasting approximately 15 to 20 seconds, which he likens to 'a seizure he once saw on television.' She did not make any sound prior to collapsing and there was no warning cry. During the event, she appeared gray and he could not palpate a pulse at the carotid for approximately 8 to 10 seconds. She then abruptly resumed spontaneous movement, gasped, and within 30 seconds was awake and asking what happened. She had no post-event confusion and did not bite her tongue. She denied urinary incontinence. The husband called 911 and EMS arrived within 6 minutes, at which point the patient was fully alert and conversational, describing only mild dizziness and 'feeling strange.' She has no prior history of seizures, no prior syncopal episodes, and no family history of sudden cardiac death or seizure disorder. She notes that she has been taking all her medications as prescribed. Approximately 5 days ago she started azithromycin for a pneumonia diagnosed by her primary care physician. Two to three days ago she also began taking ondansetron for nausea, which had been prescribed to her alongside the antibiotic. She has been on citalopram 40 mg daily for four years and hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. She denies recent changes in her other medications, illicit drug use, or ingestion of herbal supplements. On further questioning she acknowledges that she had been eating poorly due to the illness and had experienced loose stools for two days prior to presentation.
